items.value: Marginal farmers in an area organise into groups and synchronise and harmonise selected agricultural operations
items.reasoning: Small Farmer Large Field is a collectivisation-of-operations model, developed in Vietnam and promoted in India, in which small and marginal holders keep their own land and their own produce but agree to sow the same variety at the same time and to synchronise irrigation, plant protection and harvesting, so that scattered plots behave like one large field and secure economies of scale. Option C describes land leasing to a corporate body and option D describes contract farming, both of which involve an outside firm; option A describes refugee resettlement on collective farms. Only B keeps ownership with the farmers while pooling the operations.

items.value: All three are correct — niger has an MSP, is a Kharif crop, and its oil is used for cooking by tribal communities
items.reasoning: Niger seed is one of the notified crops in the Minimum Support Price list, appearing among the Kharif oilseeds alongside groundnut, soyabean, sunflower and sesamum, which settles statements 1 and 2 together. It is sown with the monsoon and harvested in the post-monsoon months. Statement 3 is correct: niger is grown largely on marginal and hill land in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh and Jharkhand, and its oil is a traditional cooking medium for tribal households there.

items.value: Three are intangible — brand recognition, intellectual property and the client mailing list; inventory is tangible
items.reasoning: An intangible asset has value without physical substance. Brand recognition, intellectual property such as patents and trademarks, and a mailing list of clients all qualify, the last because it is a data asset that can be valued and transferred. Inventory is stock in hand, a physical current asset, and is the odd one out.

items.value: Three of the five listed were used — demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal effort
items.reasoning: The Fifteenth Finance Commission's horizontal devolution formula used income distance, population, area, forest and ecology, demographic performance, and tax and fiscal effort. Excluding population, area and income distance as the question directs, three of the listed items remain: demographic performance, forest and ecology, and tax and fiscal efforts. Governance reforms and stable government were never criteria in the devolution formula, though governance-type conditions appeared in the separate context of grants.

items.value: Three — affordable housing, health care infrastructure and renewable energy; mass rapid transport is not an S3i focus area
items.reasoning: The UNOPS Sustainable Investments in Infrastructure and Innovation initiative was set up to channel institutional capital into three declared areas: affordable housing, renewable energy and health infrastructure, each chosen for its direct link to the Sustainable Development Goals. Mass rapid transport, although infrastructure, is not among the three named focus sectors. This is a narrow institutional fact rather than a derivable one, hence the reduced confidence; the runner-up is D.

items.value: Fair application of law
items.reasoning: Due process of law requires not merely that a person be deprived of life or liberty according to some enacted procedure, but that the law and its application be fair, just and reasonable, which allows a court to examine the substantive content of the law and not only its form. Option B names the opposite doctrine, the one the Indian Constitution's framers chose in Article 21 and which the courts later widened. Natural justice in option A is a component of fairness in procedure rather than the whole of the doctrine, and equality before law in option D is Article 14's guarantee against arbitrary classification, a different idea. Runner-up A.

items.value: Both correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I — the Prisons Act, 1894 placed prisons under provincial governments, which is why States run them under their own rules today
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: prisons are a State subject and each State frames its own jail manual and rules for day-to-day prison administration. Statement-II is correct in substance: the Prisons Act, 1894 is the governing statute and it confers the rule-making and administrative powers on the local or provincial government rather than the centre, which is the statutory root of the present arrangement. Because the rules States use are framed under that Act, Statement-II does explain Statement-I. The runner-up is B, for a reader who holds that the real explanation today is Entry 4 of the State List rather than the 1894 Act.

items.value: It defines and limits the powers of government
items.reasoning: The chief purpose of a constitution, in the sense of constitutionalism, is to constitute the organs of government, allocate powers among them and above all set the limits beyond which those powers may not be exercised, which is what makes a government limited rather than arbitrary. Option B captures only the constitutive half and omits the limiting half, which is the part that distinguishes a constitution from an ordinary statute. Option A describes a function of the Directive Principles and Preamble rather than the document's core purpose, and option D states a substantive goal that many but not all constitutions adopt. Runner-up B.

items.value: The 1st Amendment
items.reasoning: The First Amendment of 1951 was passed by the Provisional Parliament expressly to undo judicial readings of the Fundamental Rights: it widened the restrictions permitted on free speech under Article 19(2) after decisions such as Romesh Thappar and Brij Bhushan, added Article 15(4) to protect reservations after Champakam Dorairajan, and created Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to shield land reform laws that courts had struck down under the right to property. The 42nd Amendment was directed more broadly at curbing judicial review and elevating the Directive Principles, and is remembered chiefly as the emergency amendment rather than as a targeted reversal of Fundamental Rights case law, which makes it the runner-up.

items.value: Only one is a constitutional body — the National Commission for Backward Classes
items.reasoning: The National Commission for Backward Classes acquired constitutional status through the 102nd Constitutional Amendment of 2018, which inserted Article 338B. The National Human Rights Commission is statutory, created by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993. The National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission is statutory, created under the consumer protection legislation. The Law Commission of India is neither constitutional nor statutory; it is an executive body reconstituted by government resolution from time to time.

items.value: None of the three is correct
items.reasoning: Article 71(2) expressly saves acts done by a President in the performance of the office before the date on which the election is declared void, so statement 1 is wrong. Article 62 requires the election to be completed before the expiry of the incumbent's term, and the Supreme Court has held that an incomplete electoral college caused by dissolved Assemblies is no ground to postpone it, so statement 2 is wrong. Article 111 requires assent to be declared 'as soon as possible' when a Bill is returned but prescribes no time limit at all for the President's decision on a Bill presented for assent, so statement 3 is wrong.

items.value: Two are correct — the Rajya Sabha may amend or reject a Finance Bill and may only recommend on a Money Bill; but a joint sitting is permissive, not necessary
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: a financial bill that is not a Money Bill is otherwise an ordinary bill, so the Rajya Sabha can amend or reject it, its only disability being that such a bill cannot originate there. Statement 2 is correct and is the plain effect of Article 109, under which the Rajya Sabha may only recommend and the Lok Sabha may accept or refuse. Statement 3 is where the item turns: it is true that Article 108 excludes Money Bills from joint sittings, but for an ordinary or finance bill the President 'may' summon a joint sitting, so it is an available remedy rather than one that becomes necessary. Read strictly the answer is B; read as merely contrasting the two bill types, statement 3 passes and the answer is C, and I am genuinely split between them.

items.value: Three are correct — hunting is barred while non-timber forest produce collection and traditional agriculture continue; the Chief Wildlife Warden is not the governing authority
items.reasoning: A Community Reserve is managed by a Community Reserve Management Committee constituted for the purpose, which is the authority responsible for conserving and managing the reserve, so statement 1 is wrong. Hunting is prohibited, since the protective provisions applying to sanctuaries are extended to community reserves, so statement 2 holds. The whole point of the category is that it protects habitat without displacing people, so the continued collection of non-timber forest produce and the continuation of traditional agricultural practices in statements 3 and 4 both hold. Note a defect in the stem: community reserves are declared by the State Government under the Wild Life (Protection) Act, not by the Central Government as the lead-in asserts.

items.value: Two are correct — Scheduled Areas are notified by Presidential Order and range from a district down to a cluster of villages; the annual report is by the Governor to the President, not by Chief Ministers to the Home Ministry
items.reasoning: Statement 1 is correct: under paragraph 6 of the Fifth Schedule the President may by order declare an area to be a Scheduled Area and may alter or rescind such an order. Statement 2 matches the standard official description of the units used, in which the district is the largest unit forming a Scheduled Area and a cluster of villages within a block the smallest. Statement 3 is wrong: paragraph 3 of the Fifth Schedule places the annual reporting duty on the Governor of the State, and the report goes to the President, not from Chief Ministers to the Union Home Ministry.

items.value: Statement-I is correct but Statement-II is incorrect — Article 335 requires efficiency of administration to be maintained but nowhere defines it
items.reasoning: Statement-I is correct: from Indra Sawhney onward, and expressly in M. Nagaraj and later decisions, the Supreme Court has treated Article 335 as a limitation on the reservation power under Article 16(4), requiring that claims be considered consistently with the maintenance of efficiency of administration. Statement-II is wrong: Article 335 only uses the phrase in that qualifying clause and offers no definition of it, a silence the Court itself has commented on when observing that efficiency of administration is not a defined constitutional term.

items.value: Andhra
items.reasoning: Dhanyakataka, on the Krishna near modern Amaravati in Guntur district, was the capital region of the Satavahanas and one of the great Buddhist centres of the Andhra country, associated with the Mahasanghika school and its Chaitika and Purvasaila offshoots. Gandhara in the north-west was a Sarvastivada stronghold, Kalinga's Buddhist associations centre on Dhauli and Udayagiri, and Magadha on Rajgir, Nalanda and Bodh Gaya, none of which is Dhanyakataka.

items.value: Two are correct — the stupa held relics and served votive and commemorative purposes; but the stupa is pre-Buddhist in origin
items.reasoning: The stupa began as a burial mound raised over the remains of the dead, a practice that predates the Buddha and is attested in the earlier funerary tradition, and Buddhism adopted and elaborated the form rather than inventing it, so statement 1 is wrong. Statement 2 is correct: the classic stupa enshrines relics of the Buddha or of a venerated monk in a chamber at its core. Statement 3 is correct: stupas were raised both as votive offerings by pilgrims, which is why small votive stupas cluster around large ones, and as commemorative markers of events in the Buddha's life.

items.value: Ports
items.reasoning: All three are the great maritime outlets of the Sangam-age Tamil kingdoms: Korkai on the Tamraparni was the Pandya pearl-fishery port, Poompuhar or Kaveripattinam at the mouth of the Kaveri was the Chola port celebrated in the epics, and Muchiri, the Muziris of Graeco-Roman accounts, was the Chera port on the Malabar coast through which the pepper trade with Rome passed. The Sangam capitals were inland at Madurai, Uraiyur and Vanji, which rules out option A.

items.value: A defeated king committing ritual suicide by fasting to death
items.reasoning: The Sangam practice referred to, vadakkiruttal, literally sitting facing north, was the ritual by which a king who had been defeated or dishonoured, or who had outlived his warrior obligations, seated himself facing north and fasted until death, a formal and honourable end recorded in the Purananuru. None of the other options corresponds to a named Sangam institution of this kind. The stem prints the term as 'Vattakirutal', which appears to be a transcription variant of vadakkiruttal, and the answer is given on that reading.

items.value: None of the four was established in the early eighth century AD
items.reasoning: All four belong to the period after the tenth century. The Hoysalas rose in the Malnad region around the turn of the eleventh century and reached their height in the twelfth and thirteenth. The Gahadavalas established themselves at Kannauj in the later eleventh century. The Kakatiyas began as Chalukya feudatories and became independent under Prataparudra I in the twelfth century. The Yadavas of Devagiri likewise threw off Chalukya overlordship in the twelfth century. Not one of them is an early eighth century foundation.

items.value: Two pairs are correct — Hammira-Mahakavya by Nayachandra Suri and Nitivakyamrita by Somadeva Suri
items.reasoning: The Devichandragupta is a Sanskrit play by Vishakhadatta, the author of the Mudrarakshasa, not by Bilhana, who wrote the Vikramankadevacharita on Vikramaditya VI, so pair 1 fails. Pair 2 holds: the Hammira-Mahakavya, on Hammira of Ranthambhor, is by the Jain scholar Nayachandra Suri. Pair 3 fails: the Milindapanha records the dialogue of the Indo-Greek king Menander with the monk Nagasena, and is not the work of Nagarjuna, the later Madhyamaka philosopher. Pair 4 holds: the Nitivakyamrita, a treatise on polity, is by Somadeva Suri.

items.value: Jainism
items.reasoning: Jain cosmology holds that jiva, or soul, is present not only in animals and plants but in the elemental bodies of earth, water, fire and air, so that stones and running water possess one-sensed souls. This is the doctrinal basis of the extreme Jain practice of ahimsa, including the care taken over water, digging and fire. Buddhism denies a permanent soul altogether through the doctrine of anatta, and the Shaiva and Vaishnava traditions do not extend individual souls to rocks and streams in this way.

items.value: Devaraya I
items.reasoning: Deva Raya I is credited with damming the Tungabhadra and cutting a long canal and aqueduct to carry water into the capital, a work described by later Portuguese accounts of Vijayanagara and reflected in the hydraulic remains at Hampi, and it is the achievement for which his reign is chiefly remembered in the irrigation history of the empire. Mallikarjuna, Virupaksha and Vira Vijaya belong to the declining phase of the first dynasty and are not associated with any comparable public work.

items.value: Bahadur Shah
items.reasoning: Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, hard pressed by Humayun, sought Portuguese help and by the treaty of 1535 conceded Diu, where the Portuguese were permitted to build a fort. He later tried to reverse the concession and died in 1537 during an encounter with the Portuguese governor. Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad and Mahmud Begarha was the strongest of the Gujarat sultans, who fought the Portuguese at Chaul rather than ceding territory to them.

items.value: The Charter Act of 1833
items.reasoning: The Charter Act of 1833 redesignated the Governor General of Bengal as the Governor General of India, making William Bentinck the first holder of the new title, and vested in him exclusive legislative power for the whole of British India while stripping the Bombay and Madras presidencies of theirs. The Regulating Act of 1773 had created the post of Governor General of Bengal, Pitt's India Act of 1784 set up the Board of Control, and the Charter Act of 1793 continued existing arrangements without altering the designation.
